Shechaniah
shek-a-nī'ä
n. (a name borne by several men of the restoration; chiefly the son of Jehiel who called Israel to repentance over the strange wives)
From Hebrew Shekanyah, “the LORD hath dwelt” or “dwelling of the LORD”, from shakan, to dwell or tabernacle, with the divine name. It is a common name in the post-exilic books.

Biblical Definition

Shechaniah is one of the recurring names of the return, and its most significant bearer speaks a single sentence that changes the course of Ezra's ministry. Ezra had learned that the returned people, priests and Levites among them, had married the women of the surrounding nations, and had torn his garment and sat down astonied. It was Shechaniah who broke the silence: “And Shechaniah the son of Jehiel, one of the sons of Elam, answered and said unto Ezra, We have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives of the people of the land: yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing” (Ezr 10:2). Three things are in that sentence, and they are the anatomy of true repentance: he names the sin without softening it, he says we though his own name is not on the guilty list, and he refuses despair. Other men of the name appear across the same books — a father whose sons returned with Ezra (Ezr 8:3), the keeper of the east gate's father (Neh 3:29), and a Shechaniah of Arah whose son-in-law was Tobiah the Ammonite, a marriage alliance that gave Nehemiah's enemy ears inside Judah (Neh 6:18). The book is honest about both: the same name on the side of repentance and on the side of compromise.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Shechaniah; in sacred history it is the name of several men of the restoration, chiefly the son of Jehiel who moved Israel to put away the strange wives.

expand to see more

SHECHANIAH, n. The name signifies the LORD hath dwelt.

Shechaniah the son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam, first confessed the trespass of the strange wives.

He counselled Ezra to make a covenant with God, and said, Arise, for this matter belongeth unto thee.

Another Shechaniah is named among the chief of the fathers who went up with Ezra.

A third, of the sons of Arah, was father in law to Tobiah the enemy of Nehemiah.

Key Scripture

Ezr 10:2 — "And Shechaniah the son of Jehiel, one of the sons of Elam, answered and said unto Ezra, We have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives of the people of the land: yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing."

Ezr 8:3 — "Of the sons of Shechaniah, of the sons of Pharosh; Zechariah: and with him were reckoned by genealogy of the males an hundred and fifty."

Neh 3:29 — "After them repaired Zadok the son of Immer over against his house. After him repaired also Shemaiah the son of Shechaniah, the keeper of the east gate."

Neh 6:18 — "For there were many in Judah sworn unto him, because he was the son in law of Shechaniah the son of Arah; and his son Johanan had taken the daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah."

Modern Corruption

Ezra's reform is condemned as ethnic cleansing, and Shechaniah's confession as cruelty toward women and children; the text's own categories are religious, not racial, and the objection ignores what was actually at stake.

expand to see more

The putting away of the strange wives is the passage most often used to charge the Old Testament with racism, and the charge does not survive contact with the rest of the canon. The same Scripture makes Rahab of Jericho and Ruth of Moab mothers in the royal line, commands Israel to love the stranger, and provides in the law for a foreign woman taken into an Israelite house. What Ezra faced was not foreign blood but foreign gods: a remnant of a few thousand, newly returned from a captivity that had come upon them for idolatry, contracting the exact alliances that had produced it — and the priests leading the way. Nehemiah put the argument in one line: “Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things?” (Neh 13:26). The question was whether there would be a people left to receive the Messiah at all.

It should still be said plainly that this is a hard passage, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise: Ezra weeps, the people sit trembling in the rain, and the matter takes months to sort out family by family. The dictionary does not read it as a standing rule for the church — Paul explicitly forbids a believer to dismiss an unbelieving spouse who is willing to stay (1Co 7:12-13) — but as an extraordinary act in a unique covenant crisis. The abiding lesson is Shechaniah's, and it is about repentance rather than divorce: name the sin as ours, refuse to explain it away, and do not conclude that it is too late. “Yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing.”

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Shekanyah (H7935), Shechaniah; shakan (H7931), to dwell, tabernacle; ma'al (H4603), to trespass, act treacherously; nokri (H5237), foreign, strange; miqveh (H4723), hope.

expand to see more

Hebrew Shekanyah (H7935) — Shechaniah; the LORD hath dwelt.

Hebrew shakan (H7931) — to settle, abide, dwell; the root behind the Shekinah glory.

Hebrew ma'al (H4603) — to act unfaithfully, trespass; his word for what the people had done.

Hebrew nokri (H5237) — foreign, alien; the “strange wives” of the reform.

Hebrew miqveh (H4723) — hope, expectation; “there is hope in Israel concerning this thing”.

Usage

"“We have trespassed against our God” — a man confessing a sin that was not on his own record."

"“Yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing” — repentance that refuses despair."

"“The son in law of Shechaniah the son of Arah” — the same name inside the compromise."
